Imperative

/im-PER-uh-tiv/ - the stress falls on PER · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Imperative means absolutely necessary; a must.

The pharmacist's sticker doesn't soften it: it is imperative to finish the full course, even after the fever breaks.

Worked Example

After the gallery two doors down was robbed, the museum's security chief ended the all-staff meeting with one sentence: recoding the alarms by Friday is imperative. Not recommended, not preferred — the insurers had made plain that without new codes by the weekend, the collection stood uninsured.

Imperative is the word because the task admits no degrees and no delay: it must happen. Important things can be ranked and rescheduled; an imperative one commands — the word descends from the Latin for command — and everything else moves out of its way.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

urgent: pressing on time — act now — without imperative's claim that it must happen

vital: needed for life or success

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

optional: free to take or leave

discretionary: left to personal judgment

Where it sits · how little choice it leaves you — advisable → important → imperative

advisable vs. imperative: Advisable is a nudge — wise if convenient; imperative is an order the situation itself gives.

important vs. imperative: Important things can still be ranked, traded, and rescheduled; imperative sits above them all — the thing that must happen, full stop.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — imper-

Root — imper-: to command (Latin imperare)

Suffix — -ative

Suffix — -ative: of the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Imper- (to command — Latin imperare) + -ative = of the nature of a command. Grammar kept the plain sense: 'Sit down!' is the imperative mood, the verb form that commands. The adjective works the same way — an imperative task doesn't request your attention; it orders it.

Use the root in a new word: emperor

Use the root in a new word: emperor: The emperor's decree reached the coast before his messengers did.

Word Choice

formal / urgent

Imperative outranks its neighbors: urgent says the clock is short, important says the stakes are high, but imperative says the thing must happen — no ranking, no rescheduling. Essential, on this unit's reference list, is its closest kin; imperative adds the tone of command, which is why safety notices love it.
